## 1. Intro
- Second breakdown in the series, after Ticketmaster
- Uber: "the hardest or the most interesting" proximity search problem
  - Do this one and you can do Find My Friends, Yelp, etc.
- Asked a ton at top companies: notably Tesla, Google, Meta
- Evan: 5 years at Meta, interviewer and staff engineer
  - Asked this question "well over 50 times"
  - Knows where mid-level up to staff/principal do well or trip up
- Walks through as a real interview, with interviewer tips interjected

## 2. Roadmap
- For user-facing product designs
  1. Requirements: functional (features) + non-functional (qualities)
  2. Core entities: objects exchanged and persisted
  3. API: uses the entities to expose user-facing APIs that satisfy FRs
  4. High-level design: simply satisfy core FRs
  5. Deep dives: satisfy all NFRs

## 3. Functional requirements
- "Users should be able to…" statements
- Ideally you know the system; otherwise ask questions
- Core
  1. Riders input a start location and destination and get an estimated fare
     - E.g. UberX $32, UberXL $XYZ
  2. Riders request a ride based on an estimate, matched with a nearby available driver in real time
  3. Drivers accept/deny a request and navigate to pickup / drop-off
- Versions differ
  - Some skip fare estimate; some focus on navigation
  - This is where he typically leads candidates; not all-inclusive
- Out of scope
  - Multiple car types (only UberX: one estimate)
  - Ratings for drivers and riders
  - Scheduling rides in advance
- Tip: stay focused; at most three core features
  - Out-of-scope list shows product thinking and prioritization

## 4. Non-functional requirements
- Most candidates rush NFRs and write buzzwords
  - Not useful; doesn't help the design
- For senior and staff especially, NFRs dictate the deep dives
- Do three things
  - A. Identify qualities unique and relevant to this system (what makes it hard)
  - B. Put them in this system's context
  - C. Quantify if possible
- NFRs
  1. Low latency matching: < 1 minute to match, or failure
     - Failure = "no available drivers in the area" message
  2. Consistency of matching: ride to driver is 1:1
     - CAP: partition tolerance is a must
     - Consistency matters here, specifically for matching
     - No ride to multiple drivers, no driver getting multiple rides
  3. Highly available outside of matching
     - Minimize downtime; process requests 24/7
  4. High throughput: surges for peak hours or special events
     - Football game, Taylor Swift concert, New Year's Eve
     - Hundreds of thousands of requests within a region
- Out of scope NFRs
  - GDPR / user privacy
  - Resilience and system failures (may touch on it)
  - Monitoring, logging, alerting
  - CI/CD pipelines

## 5. On estimation
- Skipped back-of-envelope estimations on purpose
- Early estimations are "almost always a waste of time"
  - Candidates estimate DAU, bandwidth, storage, conclude "it's a lot"
  - Already knew it's scaled, horizontally scaled, maybe S3
  - Interviewer learns nothing; burns time in a ~35-minute interview
- Say instead
  - "I'd forgo estimations now and do them in HLD when the result directly influences the design. Is that okay?"
  - "99.9% of interviewers will say yes"; the "1% of weirdos" say no, then do them

## 6. Core entities
- Why "core entities", not data schema
  - Too early to know all fields; usually maps 1:1 to tables/collections
  - Full schema documented during HLD
- Entities
  - Ride
  - Driver
  - Rider
  - Location: most up-to-date location of all drivers, for proximity matching

## 7. API
- People overthink this; go one by one through FRs using entities
- Fare estimate (FR 1)
  - Requests ETA and price; persists a Ride with ETA and price
  - Reuse the Ride entity, update it later if requested
  - Unrequested estimates: excess data, but useful for analytics

```text
POST /ride/fare-estimate -> Partial<Ride>   // id, ETA, price
{ source, destination }
```

- Request ride (FR 2)
  - PATCH since it updates the same row; PUT fine too; "wouldn't get caught up"
  - Async: matching can take up to a minute

```text
PATCH /ride/request -> 200   // or 400 on failure
{ rideId }
```

- Driver location (needed for matching)
  - Drivers call every N seconds with lat/long
  - Many candidates miss it up front; fine, add it as you go

```text
POST /location/update
{ lat, long }
```

- Driver accept/deny (FR 3)
  - PATCH; could also be POST if it creates a row or different status

```text
PATCH /ride/driver/accept
{ rideId, accept: true | false }
```

- Driver navigation updates (FR 3)
  - Returns next lat/long (destination after pickup) or null after drop-off

```text
PATCH /ride/driver/update -> lat/long | null
{ rideId, status: 'pickedUp' | 'droppedOff' }
```

- No data types
  - Mid-level/junior: fine to add
  - Senior/staff: "a massive waste of time"; "borderline insulting"
  - Only spell out unique things like an enum
- No user ID in bodies
  - Comes from session / JWT in the request header
  - In body, any user could request a ride on another's behalf
  - Speak to it; maybe a bullet

## 8. HLD: fare estimate
- Timing: ideally ~15 min in by now (mid-level 15–20, senior/staff ≤ 15)
- Method: go API by API as the input data flow
- Rider client: iOS/Android; no web
- AWS managed API gateway
  - Load balancing, routing to microservices (most important)
  - Auxiliary: authentication, SSL termination, rate limiting
  - Jot them down; don't get distracted
  - Shows well on "technical excellence" axes (Meta and others)
- Ride service: handles fare estimates
  - Real Uber: complex ML model
  - Options: black box it, or oversimplify and over-communicate
  - He oversimplifies: third-party mapping (e.g. Google Maps) for ETA given traffic
  - Price = simple multiplication from ETA
- Primary DB stores the Ride

```text
Ride
- id
- riderId
- driverId?        (added later)
- fare
- eta
- source
- destination
- status: fare-estimated | matched | ...

Rider
- id
- ... (metadata, payment info)
```

- Each time an arrow lands on the DB, check for new fields
- "dot dot dot" the uninteresting parts to stay focused
- Flow: request, estimate, persist, return id + fare + ETA

## 9. HLD: request and match
- Ride matching service (separate)
  - Very different work: more computationally expensive and async
  - Scale independently; separate teams
- Location DB: current location of drivers only
  - Matching asks for drivers within N miles of the rider
- Location service
  - Driver client calls update every ~5 s
  - Writes to location DB
- Filter by driver status via a driver lookup

```text
Driver
- id
- ... (car, license plate, image)
- status: in_ride | offline | available
```

- Notification service (black boxed; itself an interview question)
  - Native push: Apple APNs; Android "Firebase, I believe"
  - "Don't quote me on that"
- Sends "do you want to accept this ride?" to driver devices

## 10. HLD: accept and navigate
- Driver taps accept: calls accept endpoint on ride service
- Update Ride: set driverId, status matched / in ride
- Driver calls update on arrival / drop-off
  - Picked up: return destination lat/long
  - Dropped off: 200, null
- Check FRs: estimates, request, accept/deny + navigate: all covered
- Open questions for deep dives
  - How does the location DB work?
  - How do we avoid double matching?

## 11. Deep dive expectations by level
- Mid-level: current board is close to passing
  - Interviewer probes matching consistency, location DB, sharding, scaling
  - Answer competently: good enough for mid-level
- Senior: go deep to satisfy NFRs, ~two places
- Staff: deeper, more places (~three)
  - Often teach the interviewer something (e.g. DynamoDB depth from experience)
  - Not required, but a fantastic sign
- He'll cover more than needed, even for staff, to show the range

## 12. Deep dive: location service and location DB
- NFR: low-latency matching
- Needs: fast proximity query + high update throughput
- Estimate (done now because it informs the design)
  - Uber has ~6M drivers; assume 3M active (probably an overestimate)
  - Update every 5 s: 3M / 5 = 600K updates/s
- Option 1: Postgres with lat and long columns
  - Range query on four bounds
  - Bad
    - B-tree indexes are optimized for one dimension; lat/long is 2D
    - Wider areas (e.g. 20 miles) scan many rows
    - Postgres handles "maybe 2–4K TPS" (depends on hardware, replicas)
    - Far from 600K
  - He'd probe even a mid-level candidate on this
- Option 2: Postgres + geospatial index + queue for batching
  - Geospatial index: makes spatial queries efficient
    - "We would use a quad tree"; Postgres extension PostGIS
  - Quad tree
    - Recursively split the map into four regions; build a tree
    - K value (example K = 5) decides whether to split a cell
    - Dense cell (7 drivers > 5) splits again
    - Query: walk down to a leaf = drivers in that cell
  - TPS: queue that batches writes to bring 600K down to ~4K
  - Downsides
    - Batching adds latency; locations become inaccurate
    - Quad tree must re-index on writes: expensive
    - Takes lots of memory
  - Okay, not great
    - Mid-level: passing; senior: he'd point out limits
    - Staff: not expected to know geo indexes deeply, but should adjust when shown limits
- Option 3 (best): Redis with geohashing
  - In-memory: "100K to, well optimized, a million" TPS in a Redis cluster
  - Geohashing: like quad trees but no extra structure to maintain
    - Recursively split into fours to a chosen precision; not density-dependent
    - Cells labeled 0–3, then 20–23, then 200–203...
    - Result is a base32-encoded string
    - Longer = more precise; prefixes give larger regions
  - Redis supports geohashing out of the box
  - Pros: cheap to compute, just a string, no extra data structure
- Quad tree vs geohash (the takeaway)
  - Quad tree: uneven density (Yelp: dense NYC, empty ocean), low update frequency
  - Geohash: density-agnostic even boxes; great for high write frequency
  - Uber: uneven density, but very high writes, so geohash
- Other options
  - Uber uses something close to geohashing but hexagons ("I believe; maybe octagons")
    - Fixes square center-to-edge vs center-to-corner distance difference
    - "I think this was built in-house at Uber"
  - Know quad tree vs geohash at this depth and you're set
- Queue is no longer needed; would be over-engineering
- Reducing 600K TPS
  - Product trade-off: update every 10, 15, 20 s, up to a minute
  - Better: dynamic location updates on the client
    - Status: not accepting rides, no updates needed
    - Speed: parked for 20 minutes, no change
    - Proximity to requests / hot areas: "out in the boonies", less often
  - Maybe 600K down to 100K or less; keep the same setup

## 13. Deep dive: consistency of matching
- Two rules
  1. Don't send more than one request at a time for a given ride
  2. Don't send any driver more than one request at a time
- Rule 1 (easy): logic inside the matching service
  - One ride is handled by one matching instance
  - Loop: next driver, send request, wait ~10 s, move on if no accept
- Rule 2 (hard): many matching instances
  - Concert ends; same closest driver for many riders on different servers
  - Driver 1 gets 100 requests at once
  - Needs coordination across instances
- Option A: driver status "request sent" in the DB
  - Check and set atomically; skip if already sent
  - Similar to Ticketmaster's no double booking
  - Problem: driver ignores request; status stuck forever
  - Cron job to reset stale statuses (needs status update time)
    - Works, but delay: cron every minute vs 5 s lock = up to 55 s idle
  - Great for mid-level; maybe passing for senior; probably not staff
- Option B (better): distributed lock with TTL
  - Redis: key driver ID, value true, TTL ~5 s (the offer window)
  - Before sending, check if driver is locked; locked, go next
  - No response: key auto-expires; driver becomes available
  - All matching instances see a consistent global view
  - Could reuse the location Redis
  - Or DynamoDB as primary DB (few relations, HA, scales "largely indefinitely")
    - Driver Lock table with driver ID and a TTL on rows
    - Consolidation; no extra technology
- Pseudocode

```text
while (noMatch) {
  driver = nextDriver
  lock(driver)
  sendNotification(driver)
  wait(10s)
}
```

- Accept comes through update; driver status to in ride; loop ends
- Notify the rider by notification, polling, or otherwise (not detailed)

## 14. Deep dive: surges
- Can't autoscale matching instances fast enough for a surge
- Add a ride request queue in front of matching
  - Requests wait; matching pulls when ready
- FIFO problem: a hard-to-match rider ("in the boonies") blocks easy NYC ones
- Partition the queue by region (finer than boroughs)
- Bonus: a matching instance that dies mid-match
  - Message not acknowledged; another instance picks it up

## 15. Deep dive: availability outside matching
- Horizontally scale each service behind load balancers
- DynamoDB primary scales "largely indefinitely"; Redis scaling covered
- Split by region
  - Full stack copy per region (northeast, southwest, northwest) in different data centers
  - Travelers: user table replicated / read replica in every region
  - Also makes queue partitioning more natural

## 16. Wrap-up by level
- Went into more detail than an interview needs; don't feel overwhelmed
- Mid-level: HLD + answer deep-dive questions: doing great
- Senior: deep in a couple places (location service, matching)
  - Even landing on cron job, or queue + PostGIS quad trees: likely a hire
- Staff: higher bar; more depth, maybe in places you know better than him

## 17. Board
- Exported Excalidraw board from the video

![Excalidraw board from the video](data:image/png;base64,)

- Text version, assembled from the talk
  - FR: fare estimate; request ride; driver accept/deny + navigate
  - NFR: matching < 1 min or fail; ride:driver 1:1; HA outside matching; surges 100s of K per region
  - Entities: Ride, Driver, Rider, Location
  - Numbers: 6M drivers, 3M active, 3M / 5 = 600K TPS; Redis 100K–1M TPS

```text
Rider app ---\                               3rd-party mapping
              API gateway --> Ride Service ------- Primary DB (DynamoDB: Ride, Driver, Driver Lock TTL)
Driver app --/   |  requestRide()
 (dynamic        +--> Ride Request Queue --> Ride Matching Service --> Location DB (Redis geohash)
  updates)       +--> Location Service ---------------------------------^
Notification Service (APNs, Firebase) --> Driver app
```

  - Quad tree (K = 5): pros = efficient bounding-box search; cons = complex, more storage
  - Geohash: pros = single string, prefix proximity, uniform; cons = precision varies by latitude, boundary issue (neighbors may not share a prefix)
